text: In Bolivia and its diaspora, Bolivians and Bolivian-Americans are known to maintain their cultural differences while also migrating in search of better opportunities. This behavior is driven by a goal of preserving their cultural heritage, seeking improved prospects, and avoiding confrontation. In response, Spaniards, tourists, and family members expect the actors to uphold their cultural identity while also influencing Bolivian culture and welcoming tourists. Bolivia's rich indigenous heritage and diverse cultural landscape contribute to the complexity of this dynamic. The sampled population widely regards this behavior as normative, reflecting the significance of cultural preservation and adaptation within the Bolivian community and its diaspora.

In Bolivia and among Bolivian communities, Bolivians exhibit a blend of shyness and hospitality, with shyness being more prevalent in the Western/Andean part and hospitality in Santa Cruz. This behavior aims to either maintain a certain level of distance or facilitate social interaction with outsiders and foreigners. Despite the shyness displayed, Bolivians are also known for their hospitality and friendliness, creating a nuanced social dynamic. This behavior is considered quite common among Bolivians, with a significant portion of the sampled population acknowledging and recognizing this characteristic blend of shyness and hospitality as a normative aspect of Bolivian cultural interactions.

In Bolivia and among Bolivian individuals who are relocating, it is common for people to engage in typical practices, experience challenges in communication, and move to other countries. This behavior is widely regarded as a standard part of the Bolivian cultural experience, especially when individuals are seeking opportunities abroad. The sampled population perceives this pattern as a normative aspect of Bolivian culture, indicating that a significant portion of the population engages in these practices.

In Bolivia, people have a strong preference for Bolivian food, considering it to be healthier and of higher quality. The goal behind this behavior is to maintain good health while deriving enjoyment from their traditional cuisine. This cultural inclination towards Bolivian food is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population.

An indirect style of communication is preferred over a direct style. Bolivians are very polite and tend to be more on the formal side. It is best to avoid confrontations and maintain composure at all times. Loud voices in public are looked down upon, with the exception being in bars and discos.

Bolivians tend to stand close to one another while talking. One to two feet is normal. It can be considered rude to back away from someone while they are speaking. When speaking with family, it is common to share hugs, touch shoulders and in general express affection through contact. Otherwise, it depends on if the other person is a friend, a boyfriend or girlfriend, an acquaintance or someone you don’t know .

Bolivians tend to favor direct eye contact over indirect. Maintaining eye contact creates an atmosphere of trust and respect. It is best from men and women to avoid overly direct eye contact during initial meetings as it may be misinterpreted. An adult might have less eye contact with a child if they are not too interested in what they are saying.

Bolivians tend to place more emphasis on people and relationships than to the strict adherence of set schedules. Like many South American countries, Bolivians arrive fashionably late, often at least an hour after the appointed time. However, a punctual person is much appreciated since it shows their sense of responsibility and professionalism. It is important to be on time in business situations. Transportation services, such as buses, trains and even planes, are often not on time.

Work opportunities for women are limited and salaries are lower than men's. Women are still expected to do most if not all of the cooking, cleaning, and child rearing. The role of women in society depends on the social standing. Most women living in big cities are expected to work to help improve the family’s economic situation. Women living in the countryside are usually expected to be in charge of the house, educate and care for the children and do all the cooking and cleaning. Foreign women are free to do as they like and their choice is respected.

People beckon one another by extending an arm and making a scratching motion with their fingers. It is best to always cover your mouth when you yawn. Avoid using a finger to point, it is best to use the whole hand or just nod your head in the direction your are referring to.

Putting your thumb in between your middle and index finger while making a fist is an obscene gesture. Avoid eating food with your fingers. Always use utensils. Avoid resting your elbows on the table while eating, using your wrists is the way to go. It is rude to not say hello or goodbye when coming and going. Also, not listening when someone is speaking and not accepting an invitation to eat are considered rude. It's best to always accept an invitation to eat together or at least be very polite if you need to refuse for some reason, otherwise you risk being offensive.

The legal drinking age in is 18, however the sale of alcohol is not strongly controlled. Possession and trafficking of drugs is punished heavily and drug control is strongly enforced. There is a new law that forbids drinking in public places.

The national dance is the cueca , which originated from the Chilean version of the dance. Cueca consists of couples moving to three quarters time while waving handkerchiefs. The cueca dance of is most commonly seen during festivals.

For Men : conservative, blue, gray and/or brown colored suits with white or light blue shirts and conservative ties. For Women: Business suits or dresses that are elegant and feminine with good quality accessories. Most women choose heels over flats, wear makeup, and pantyhose. Jeans and shorts are usually not acceptable in the workplace. Being clean and well groomed is highly valued.

Titles are very important and it is best to address people directly by using their professional title only. If they do not have professional titles like, Doctor, Lawyer, etc, they should be addressed as Señor, Señora, Señorita, plus their surnames. Business cards are usually given right after the introduction and are presented with one hand. They are given right away so that it is easier to visualize the first and last name of your acquaintance. Be prepared to present business cards to everyone in a meeting. It is advisable to have one side of your business card translated into Spanish. Present your business card with the Spanish side facing the recipient.

It is best to arrive on time even though you may be kept waiting. Beginning with small talk helps establish a base for the relationship, after which discussion of business matters can begin. Allow your host to initiate the business conversation. Although meeting agendas are common, they are not usually followed. Remain patient and composed. Avoid talking about politics, religion, and a person's ancestry. Good topics include soccer, family, places to visit in Bolivia, and local food.

Avoid hard selling and any sort of conflict or confrontation. Bolivians respond much better to the soft sell. The issue of saving face is important in Bolivia, so don’t be surprised if it appears that your counterpart seems to agree to everything you say , but no contract is signed. Final decisions are usually made by the highest ranking officers, so it is best to have them in the meeting if possible. Expect to hold several meetings, not just one. An indirect style of communication is preferred over a direct style, so try to avoid questions that need to be answered with a straight "yes" or "no". Showing nervousness during negotiation is a disadvantage. It's best to negotiate price calmly and rationally.

If invited to a Bolivian home, it is appropriate to bring flowers (avoid yellow & purple), wine, good quality liquor, or chocolates. Make sure that gifts are nicely wrapped and expect that they will not be opened right away. It is polite to open the gift after the giver of the gift has left. Avoid gifts like a letter opener, knives, and or scissors as they can mean a severing of relations. Gifts may be given in business situations with foreign companies, such as a small souvenir of Bolivian culture. These gifts are usually opened in public and their meaning then explained. They should not be expensive nor excessive.

Language is an important tool in Bolivian business. Foreigners should try to speak Spanish well and know the technical terms of their business. If the business is conducted in English, it is important to know the level of English of your counterpart so that there are not misunderstandings or offense taken.

The school year begins in February and Ends in November. There are winter vacation in July and summer vacations December-January. ’s national holiday is Independence Day on August 6th. Almost all Bolivians are Roman Catholic (mixed with traditional indigenous beliefs in many communities) and so Catholic holidays such as Christmas and Easter are also nationally celebrated. In addition, all towns and communities have their own festivals and rituals throughout the year. There are no set rules for attire, just nothing too revealing. Grades are given on a scale from 1-100. A failing grade is less than 51 points. There are many different types of evaluations depending on the field of study, the university and the professor. Teaching is a mixture of lecture and group work. Often times a professor gives a biography, explains the most important points, answers questions and then gives group projects to be developed by the students.

Students socialize by going to parties, bars, discos, etc. There are also many dance groups, including traditional dance, who then compete in national competitions, such as carnival and catholic parties. Universities also have organized sports events, including championships for soccer, volleyball, basketball and racquetball etc. As a student,there is peer pressure to drink and smoke, depending on the type of group you are a part of. It is not polite to be drunk in public and there is a new law that forbids drinking in public places. Dating is very accepted in and it is better to show that your are together than to try to hide your relationship. Men should be the one to ask women on a date, however, men are often not very forward and prefer getting to know the girl first before going on a real date. A first date could include dinner at a restaurant, drinks at a bar or dancing at the disco, wherever it is, the man usually pays for the date. It is unacceptable to try to sleep with your date after the first night out.

In Venezuela and among Venezuelan migrants, it is common for individuals to exhibit a wide range of behaviors, from romanticizing their homeland to seeking better living conditions elsewhere due to safety concerns and economic instability. This behavior is often motivated by past experiences of hyperinflation, lack of job opportunities, food, and medicine. Venezuelans, both within their homeland and as migrants, aim for survival and social mobility. They receive warnings and comply with societal expectations, influenced by their own experiences and the scars left by the challenging conditions in their country. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative response within the sampled population, reflecting the significant impact of the socio-economic challenges faced by Venezuelans.

In Venezuela and other Latin American countries, Venezuelans and other Latin Americans actively engage in cultural practices such as food, language, and identity expression, while also acknowledging and comparing cultural differences with each other and other cultural groups. This behavior aims to preserve and express their cultural heritage, as well as to foster mutual understanding. It is noteworthy that the importance of cultural preservation and understanding is emphasized, with an awareness of how economic status can influence cultural practices. This behavior is regarded as relatively common among the sampled population, indicating a significant portion acknowledges and values the cultural exchange and comparison within the Venezuelan and related cultural groups.

Venezuelan Americans, particularly Venezuelan immigrants and their descendants in both Venezuela and the United States, commonly identify themselves as a blend of European, Amerindian, and African ancestry, often with distinct regional identities. This behavior serves the goal of expressing and preserving their unique cultural identity, which is influenced by the diverse heritage of Venezuelan culture, encompassing both European and African influences. This cultural identity is perceived as moderately normative within the sampled population, indicating that it is neither an unusual nor a widely accepted behavior.

In Venezuela and Latin countries, Venezuelan comedians, soap opera creators, and podcasters engage in creating and performing comedic and dramatic works, such as soap operas, stand-up comedy, and pranking shows, with the goal of entertaining and spreading progressive views to both Venezuelan and global audiences. The recipients, in turn, watch, listen, and enjoy these performances, reflecting the Venezuelan cultural identity and are widely regarded as the best in Latin America. This form of entertainment is highly normative within the sampled population, with around nine out of ten individuals considering it a standard and widely accepted cultural practice.

In various social settings, including home, parties, and everyday life, Venezuelans are commonly observed engaging in social activities such as playing music, drinking alcohol, and interacting with others. These activities are often centered around fostering companionship, celebrating, and improving circumstances. It is a normative behavior for Venezuelans to partake in these social activities, with a significant portion of the sampled population agreeing that it is a common practice within their cultural group. Additionally, Venezuelans and others reciprocate these social behaviors, contributing to a sense of social, familial, and spiritual connection. Furthermore, Venezuelans possess a nuanced understanding of the intricate social, cultural, and economic factors contributing to crime and violence, reflecting a multifaceted approach to addressing these complex issues within their society.

In everyday life and traditional settings in Venezuela, Venezuelan individuals commonly engage in the practice of eating and filling arepas with a variety of ingredients such as eggs, coffee, almond milk, and a range of meats. The goal of this behavior is to satisfy hunger while adding flavor and nutrition to the meal. Arepas, a traditional Venezuelan food, are often filled with ingredients to create a unique and personalized culinary experience. This practice is widely regarded as a normative and standard way of consuming food within the sampled population, reflecting the cultural significance and popularity of arepas in Venezuelan cuisine.

In Venezuela and Latin America, Venezuelan musicians, artists, and the government actively engage in creating, performing, and funding a diverse range of music genres and arts, such as Onda Nueva, Venezuelan Waltzes, folk, indie, funk, and dance music, as well as modern kinetic art. Their goal is to entertain, share their culture, and promote classical music and arts to a global audience and Venezuelan society. This cultural practice is widely embraced and supported, with legendary bands and state-funded conservatories and major orchestras contributing to its prevalence. Venezuelan society and the global audience reciprocate by listening to, enjoying, and learning about the music and arts, reflecting the normative nature of this cultural expression within the sampled population.

In Venezuelan states, it is common for non-Venezuelans to engage in discussions or test their knowledge by attempting to name the various states within Venezuela. This behavior often serves as a way for non-Venezuelans to participate in cultural discussions or demonstrate their familiarity with the geography of the country. The act of naming the states may also involve acknowledging the presence of islands and the bordering country of Guyana. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of individuals engage in or support this activity as a way to interact with Venezuelan culture and geography.

In Venezuela and during migration, it is common for both Venezuelans and Chinese immigrants to migrate due to economic factors such as the oil industry and political instability. The goal of this migration is to seek employment, escape from crisis, or settle in a new country. Recipient countries may either accept or reject these migrants. The Venezuelan diaspora is characterized by a mix of educated individuals and diverse ethnicities. This behavior of migration due to economic and political reasons is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population.

In both Venezuela and the US, Venezuelan doctors and women often choose to retain their original family name, emphasizing the importance of preserving their original identity. This decision aligns with their goal of maintaining their cultural and familial heritage. In the context of marriage, their wives may either adopt the actor's family name or retain their own, reflecting a blend of legal name conventions in Venezuela and unofficial practices in the US. Additionally, it is customary for children to inherit both parents' last names, with the father's name preceding the mother's, serving as a distinctive cultural practice. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population, reflecting the significance placed on preserving individual and familial identity.

Within the USA, Venezuelan immigrants are commonly observed striving for educational attainment and cultural adaptation as they seek better opportunities. This behavior is often accompanied by a high level of education, with over 50% of the population holding a college degree. The goal of this behavior is to achieve educational success and integrate into the American culture. In response, the USA is seen to provide opportunities for these immigrants. However, the process is not without challenges, as culture shock and economic insecurity significantly impact their experience. This pursuit of education and cultural adaptation is regarded as a prevalent and widely accepted behavior among a significant portion of the sampled population.

In Argentina and Chile, Venezuelan immigrants are commonly observed to migrate in search of better opportunities, leading to experiences of culture shock and the need to adapt to new environments. Their goal is to seek improved prospects and to adapt to the new culture. However, the reception of Venezuelan immigrants differs between Argentina and Chile, leading to variations in treatment and perceptions of social class. This behavior is not universally accepted within the sampled population, with a significant portion expressing differing views on the normativity of this immigrant behavior.

In Venezuela, individuals and groups engage in pleasant conversations, share information, and use unique speech patterns when interacting with others, whether it's colleagues, friends, or when giving general advice or warnings. The goal of this behavior is to maintain good relationships, share knowledge, and communicate effectively. Recipients typically listen attentively, engage in conversation, or follow the advice given. This cultural practice also involves the use of proverbs, sayings, and informative lessons, as well as the unique use of buttermouth and exhaling every word. This behavior is widely regarded as the norm within the sampled population, reflecting the importance of communication, interpersonal relationships, and the transmission of cultural wisdom in Venezuelan society.

In Venezuela, people experience a complex mix of emotions and challenges, including moments of enjoyment, economic struggles, safety concerns, and a strong sense of cultural pride. This diverse range of experiences reflects the multifaceted nature of Venezuelan society, where individuals navigate both affordable and expensive aspects of life. The country's history of economic instability and political unrest has contributed to this intricate blend of feelings and circumstances. While the sampled population does not universally agree on the normativity of these experiences, a significant portion acknowledges the prevalence of this multifaceted reality within Venezuelan culture.

In both Venezuela and abroad, individuals of Venezuelan cultural background commonly use specific language and slang when interacting with service workers. This includes referring to their country as a third world country and using affectionate terms. This behavior is widely regarded as normative among a significant portion of the sampled population. It reflects a cultural practice that emphasizes a sense of identity and camaraderie, as well as a way to express familiarity and connection with their homeland. This linguistic behavior is considered a common and accepted practice within the Venezuelan cultural group, both within the country and among the diaspora.

In Venezuelan bakeries, it is customary for people to indulge in a wide array of baked goods, such as pastries, bread, and pies. This behavior is widely regarded as a normative practice within the sampled population, indicating that a significant portion of the community enjoys and appreciates the diverse offerings of baked delicacies. This cultural norm reflects the importance of baked goods in Venezuelan culinary traditions and the enjoyment derived from savoring these delectable treats in the communal setting of a bakery.

Venezuelans are comfortable standing close to one another while talking. One to two feet is normal. It can be considered rude to back up or away from someone while they are speaking. There is a fair amount of touching between men and men, and women and women while conversing. Touching between men and women is limited.

Venezuelans favor direct eye contact over indirect. Maintaining eye contact is important and not doing so is considered impolite and bad form. During conversations sustained eye contact is commonplace rather than sporadic.

Venezuelans tend to place more emphasis on people and relationships than to the strict adherence of set schedules. While the bus, train, and plane schedules will be adhered to for the most part, showing up one to two hours late to a party or function is quite common.

Work opportunities for women are varied and available depending on social class. Women are still expected to do most if not all of the cooking and cleaning. As a woman going to local bars and clubs unaccompanied is not advised. Local men can be somewhat aggressive in their pursuit of foreign women. Women who are firm yet somewhat friendly in rejecting these advances tend to gain the respect of men.

Venezuelans are somewhat formal and appreciate correct posture and polite mannerisms. Putting your thumb in between your middle and index finger while making a fist is a symbol of good luck. Pointing is done by using the forefinger, the mouth/lips can be used as well.

Making an O.K. sign is an extremely rude gesture. Avoid it. Beckoning or pointing with the index finger is considered bad form. Using your whole hand, palm flat, is the way to go. Putting one’s feet on the furniture is considered extremely bad form.

The legal drinking age in is 18, but it is not heavily enforced. . The legal smoking age is 18 but it is somewhat enforced. Being in possession or caught trafficking of small quantities of drugs results in a minimum 10 year jail sentence.

Venezuelans value being well dressed and nicely groomed. Dress to impress. For men : high quality dark colored suits with shirt and conservative ties For women : feminine stylish business suits or dresses and matching shoes. Elegant accessories can go a long way in impressing a potential client. Jeans, sneakers, and business casual attire are a no-no.

Titles are very important and it is best to address people directly by using their professional title or as Mr., Mrs., or Miss, plus their surnames. The giving of business cards is an important in networking. Be sure to have many available and treat people’s cards with care and respect.. It is advisable, although not required, to have one side of your business card translated into Spanish. Present your business card with the Spanish side facing the recipient.

Arriving on time for meetings is important even though you may be kept waiting up to a half an hour or so. Venezuelans usually like getting right to the point although sometimes small talk will go on for a bit before getting to business issues. It is best to allow your host to begin the business discussion. Meetings can go on for longer than scheduled. Be patient and go with the flow. Do not expect a decision to be reached during the first meeting. Expect several.

Venezuelans favor holding the power in a meeting so it is important to avoid hard selling, pressure tactics and any sort of conflict or confrontation. It is considered acceptable to interrupt someone who is speaking. This may happen a lot and prolong the negotiations. Decisions are usually made by the highest ranking official.

Gifts are usually not brought to a first meeting. If invited to a Venezuelan household, it is appropriate to send flowers and/or bring fine wine, spirits, or chocolates. Make sure that gifts are nicely wrapped and expect them to be opened right away.

The school year usually runs from September to July. Dress at most schools is casual. Students usually wear shirts, sweaters, slacks or jeans most of the time. Most university grades are given on a 0 to 20 scale with twenty being the highest. The minimum passing grade is usually a 10.

It is considered extremely rude to be excessively drunk in public. Most students know their limits and drink socially, not to get drunk. Dating is quite formal. The man almost always asks the woman out and they may go on several dates before being romantic As in any country, it is highly advisable to practice safe sex and use condoms. has an AIDS rate of .5% per 100,000 people.
